title: Rabbi Shmuel Mohilever
content:
Rabbi Samuel Mohilever

The text surveys the multifaceted figure of Rabbi Samuel Mohilever, one of the founding fathers of Religious Zionism, tracing his work that combined Lithuanian Torah scholarship with pioneering national activism. The article opens with his biographical background as a Torah prodigy and details the stations of his life as a communal rabbi, which prepared him to bridge social divides and develop the vision of settling the Land of Israel through natural means. A central axis in the writing focuses on his practical initiatives, ranging from recruiting Baron Rothschild to the settlement enterprise and establishing the moshava Mazkeret Batya, to formulating the heter mekhira (sale dispensation) in the Sabbatical year of 5649 (1889) as a halakhic solution ensuring the survival of Hebrew agriculture. Additionally, his leadership role in establishing the Mizrahi movement and founding a theology of partnership with the secular public for the national goal is explained. The text concludes with a historiographic survey of his Torah writings that were lost in pogroms and fires, and emphasizes how his legacy continues to shape modern Jewish identity uniting fidelity to halakha with national revival.

Halakhic Leadership, National Diplomacy, and Zionist Doctrine: The Life's Work and Torah Thought of Rabbi Samuel Mohilever

The Biographical Background and Development of a Torah Leader

Rabbi Samuel Mohilever, born in the town of Głębokie near Vilna in 5584 (1824) and deceased on 19 Sivan 5658 (1898), represents one of the most influential junctures in modern Jewish history.[1, 2] His figure powerfully combines the pronounced Torah scholarship of the Lithuanian Mitnagdic school with a deep affinity for the idea of redemption, rooted in part in his family lineage.[1] Rabbi Mohilever was born to a distinguished family of Torah luminaries spanning twenty-two generations; his father, Rabbi Yehuda Leib, was a Mitnagdic rabbi and merchant, while his mother belonged to a renowned Hasidic family.[1] This cultural and spiritual fusion between Lithuanian rationalist scholarship and Hasidic fervor constituted a critical psychological and intellectual foundation in shaping his personality as a leader capable of bridging deep social and ideological divides within the Jewish people.[1, 2] His original family name was Mohilever, after the city of Mogilev, but the name was corrupted by those who had difficulty pronouncing it and became Mohilever.[2]

Already in his youth he was known as an exceptional prodigy and was called "the prodigy of Głębokie," and independently acquired extensive knowledge in the history of the Jewish people and general sciences.[1] After his marriage at age fifteen, he engaged in teaching gemara with Rashi and Tosafot to the youth of his town for approximately three years.[1] At an age not exceeding eighteen, he turned to formal study at the prestigious Volozhin yeshiva, where he received rabbinic ordination within only six months.[1] Like his forebears, he initially refused to earn his living from the rabbinate and engaged in the flax trade, but following a plague in which his wife's parents perished in 5608 (1848) and his business began to collapse, he acceded to the entreaties of his community members and accepted upon himself the yoke of the rabbinate.[1]

The various rabbinic positions in which he served throughout his life provided fertile ground for developing his public conception and the social cohesion he preached, as detailed in the following table:

This process of movement between communities of diverse character granted Rabbi Mohilever a profound understanding of the Jewish social mosaic in Eastern Europe, and prepared him to become one of the founding fathers of Religious Zionism.[1, 2]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The National Turning Point, the Pawłówka Initiative, and the Establishment of Mazkeret Batya

Rabbi Mohilever's active national awakening began in 1874, with the founding of the "Mazkeret Moshe" fund in honor of the ninetieth birthday of Sir Moses Montefiore.[2, 4] Rabbi Mohilever enlisted enthusiastically in fundraising for the fund, and from then on the idea of settling the Land of Israel became the central axis of his life and occupation.[2, 4] With the outbreak of the "Storms in the South" pogroms (1881–1882), he became one of the founders and prominent leaders of the Ḥovevei Tzion movement.[2, 5] He participated actively in the historic Kattowitz Conference in 1884, which laid the practical and organizational foundations of the movement.[3]

One of the historic breakthroughs attributed to his diplomatic activity is his direct and personal approach to Baron Edmond James de Rothschild in Paris.[3, 6] The foundational meeting was held on the first day of the festival of Sukkot 5643 (1882), when Rabbi Mohilever, out of strict observance of the sanctity of the festival, walked on foot for approximately two hours to the Baron's home.[6] In this meeting the Rabbi succeeded in moving the Baron's heart and presenting to him a grounded vision of Jewish agricultural settlement in the ancestral land, thereby enlisting him to assist the immigrants of the First Aliyah.[3, 4] The Baron agreed to the initiative, on condition that families with actual agricultural experience be located who would be willing to immigrate to the Land of Israel of their own volition and at their own expense.[5]

Following this agreement, Rabbi Mohilever located ten families of Jewish peasants in the village of Pawłówka in Poland, who had been tillers of the soil from their youth.[5] The men immigrated to the Land, underwent rigorous agricultural training at the "Mikveh Israel" agricultural school, and after they proved their skill as farmers, the Baron established a moshava for them and they brought up their families.[5] The moshava was founded at the end of 1883 under the name Ekron, and was later called "Mazkeret Batya" after the Baron's mother.[3, 5, 7] The Mazkeret Batya Museum today displays a reconstruction of living quarters, kitchen utensils, and details from this period perpetuating the Rabbi's work.[8]

Rabbi Mohilever's practical activity was not confined to the European arena; in 1890 he visited the Land of Israel, actively assisted in establishing the moshava Reḥovot [3], and even presented an early and bold vision for Jewish settlement in the Beirut area and in the north of the Land.[9] His long-term influence was perpetuated, inter alia, in Kibbutz Gan Shmuel, whose origin was an etrog orchard planted in his honor in 5656 as an expression of the spiritual and agricultural connection between the Diaspora and the Land of Israel.[3, 10] The etrogim of the Land of Israel were perceived as superior in terms of their intrinsic and spiritual value among Diaspora Jews, but the orchard became diseased, and subsequently orange trees were planted in its place and soon thereafter the kibbutz bearing his name was established.[10]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

His Torah Thought and Halakhic Legacy

The doctrine of Rabbi Samuel Mohilever is based on a unique synthesis between pure halakha and a modern historical-national conception. He viewed the Torah of Israel as the source of life and the moral infrastructure of the nation, but held that the revival of the people in their land must be accomplished through practical and natural means.[2]

The Beginning of Redemption Through Natural Means and Settlement of the Land

Like other Zionist precursors of his generation, such as Rabbi Tzvi Hirsch Kalischer, Rabbi Mohilever held the conception that the future redemption would not occur in a miraculous and sudden manner, but in a gradual and natural process ("little by little").[2] According to this approach, the historic duty of the Jewish people is to actively initiate its return to the Land, to acquire lands, to build houses, to plant vineyards, and to sow fields.[2] Relying on the Ramban's method in Sefer Ha-Mitzvot, Rabbi Mohilever ruled that the commandment of settling the Land of Israel is a positive commandment for all generations, equivalent in weight to the entire Torah, and that it constitutes the foundation of the physical and spiritual existence of the nation.[2, 11]

Alongside this, the Rabbi presented a complex and gradated halakhic doctrine regarding the question of residence in the Land of Israel versus the Diaspora, based on observance of the Torah:

One who has the ability to dwell in the Land of Israel and observe there Torah and commandments—it is incumbent upon him to dwell in the Land of Israel.[12]

One who fears that in the Land of Israel he will be unable to observe Torah and commandments properly, but outside the Land he will be able to observe them without concern—it is preferable that he dwell outside the Land.[12]

One who in no place, whether in the Land or abroad, is able to observe Torah and commandments—let him dwell outside the Land and sit alone in his home.[12]
This position clarifies that despite his Zionist fervor, observance of Torah and commandments remained the supreme criterion and the foundation for any national edifice in the Land of the Fathers.[2, 12]

The Theology of Partnership with the Secular

One of the most complex challenges Rabbi Mohilever confronted was the polemic over national partnership.[2] Various Haredi and rabbinic circles refused to cooperate with the pioneers of the First Aliyah and the maskilim, the majority of whom did not observe Torah and commandments with piety.[2] Rabbi Mohilever developed a bold and tolerant theological doctrine, based on profound midrashic sources:

The principle of the primacy of the Land: The rabbi relied on the midrash in Sifrei Devarim and Eikha Rabbah which brings the words of the Holy One, blessed be He: "Would that my people were in the Land of Israel even though they defile it."[12] From this he concluded that residence in the Land of Israel and its physical construction are preferable in the eyes of the Creator over meticulous observance of commandments in the Diaspora.[12]

Non-abstention from performing a commandment because of transgressors: He emphasized that one must not nullify or boycott a holy national commandment such as building up the Land merely because non-religious people participate in it.[12] He compared this to the erev rav (mixed multitude) that ascended with Moses in the wilderness and did not prevent the people's arrival at the Land.[12]

Acceptance of every Jew unconditionally: The rabbi supported the acceptance of every Jew into the ranks of the Ḥovevei Tsiyon movement, without any halakhic qualification regarding observance of the commandments.[2] He operated through two parallel channels: defense of the status of religion and the religious pioneers in the moshavot, and conversely—rapprochement and persuasion among the maskil and secular leadership.[2]

This conception enabled him to develop a close and warm relationship with Binyamin Ze'ev Herzl.[2] Rabbi Mohilever greatly valued his book Der Judenstaat and in his letters called Herzl "the distinguished and most exalted man," while Herzl for his part saw the rabbi as a strategic partner of the first rank and defined himself as continuing his path.[2]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Polemic over the Shemittah of 5649 and the Halakhic Arrangement

The greatest halakhic test of the practical religious-Zionist approach came toward the shemittah year of 5649 (1888–1889).[13] This was the first shemittah year in which the new agricultural moshavot faced the challenge of absolute cessation of work.[13, 14] The communities of the Old Yishuv in Jerusalem viewed the observance of shemittah in its plain sense as a condition for redemption and as a way to draw down divine blessing, and opposed any compromise.[13, 15]

Rabbi Mohilever, together with a handful of rabbis supporting settlement, identified that complete cessation of agricultural work would necessarily lead to the absolute economic collapse of the young moshavot and to real danger to life for the pioneers.[13, 14] From a dynamic halakhic perspective combining classical adjudication with national responsibility, Rabbi Mohilever together with his colleagues formulated the foundations of the "heter mekhirah" (sale permit), whose roots rest on ancient rulings of the sages of Safed from approximately five hundred years earlier.[13, 15] The permit is based on temporary sale of the lands of the Land of Israel to a non-Jew, thereby temporarily removing the sanctity of the land and permitting certain types of work to be performed on it (primarily by non-Jewish laborers).[13, 14]

The halakhic and public polemic was extremely stormy, and divided the Torah world into two clear camps:

This permit, despite the fierce criticism it absorbed, constituted the cornerstone that enabled Hebrew agriculture to survive its first years, and became an inseparable part of the map of halakhic adjudication of religious Zionism for its generations.[13, 14]

This polemic has received comprehensive historical studies over the years, analyzing the variety of religious and social aspects of the affair:

In broad historical perspective, the discussion surrounding the permit continues to this day, as modern decisors such as Rabbi Mordechai Eliyahu and Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Auerbach permitted its use post facto.[17] Conversely, rabbis such as Rabbi Ya'akov Ariel and Rabbi Ze'ev Weitman expressed concern that transforming the permit into a permanent matter might remove the sanctity of the Land, while Rabbi Meir Mazuz ruled that one should be lenient and permit it ab initio in situations where vegetable prices through alternative channels such as otzar beit din are too high for the public.[17]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Establishment of a "Spiritual Center" (Mizraḥi) and Confronting the Movement's Crises

In the year 5653 (1893) the Ḥovevei Tsiyon movement fell into a deep crisis: several settlement attempts failed, the Ottoman authorities imposed severe decrees on immigration and land acquisition, and the movement's leader Dr. Yehudah Leib Pinsker died.[2] Simultaneously, the publication of the piercing articles of Ahad Ha'am ("Truth from the Land of Israel") undermined many people's confidence in the righteousness of the path, and opposition to the national vision intensified both from extremist Haredi circles and from secular maskilim.[2]

In response to this crisis, Rabbi Mohilever initiated a special assembly of the movement's leaders in the spa town of Druskininkai in the month of Elul 5653.[2] At this assembly it was decided to establish a new center for advocacy and leadership under Rabbi Mohilever's leadership, which was called "Merkaz Ruḥani" (Spiritual Center) and in abbreviation—Mizraḥi.[2, 3] This movement constituted the historical and ideological foundation upon which Rabbi Yitsḥak Ya'akov Reines later established the worldwide "Mizrachi" movement within the framework of the Zionist Organization.[2, 3]

The Fate of His Torah Writings and Reconstruction Efforts

One of the most complex aspects in the historiography of Rabbi Mohilever is the fate of his Torah writings.[18] Throughout his life the rabbi composed dozens of extensive halakhic and philosophical treatises, reflecting his immense erudition and his innovative approach.[18, 19]

The First Loss of Writings (1906) and the Scope of the Loss

After the rabbi's death, his close associate and student Rabbi Yitsḥak Nissenbaum worked to have his halakhic writings printed.[18] The public purpose was clear: to prove beyond doubt his unassailable Torah greatness of Rabbi Mohilever, and thereby to repel the claims of opponents of Ḥibbat Tsiyon who tried to present him as a public activist lacking halakhic stature.[18] Rabbi Nissenbaum requested from the executive committee of the Zionist movement funding of one thousand rubles (through the purchase of one thousand photographs of the rabbi that remained in their possession), but the request was rejected.[18] As a result, the writings remained in manuscript and were completely burned during the savage pogroms carried out against the Jews of Białystok in the year 5666 (1906).[18]

The scope of the Torah treasury that was lost was enormous, and according to Rabbi Nissenbaum's testimony from the year 5680 (1920) included more than two hundred printed pages of responsa on the four parts of the Shulḥan Arukh, novellae and commentaries on nearly all of the Babylonian Talmud and on Ḥoshen Mishpat, profound homilies on topics of talmudic ethics and Jewish philosophy, complex halakhic responsa on the laws of pe'ah and kil'ayim based on complex geometric and engineering calculations, a long and comprehensive halakhic responsum detailing the foundations of the shemittah permit, and a long-term Hebrew calendar corresponding with mathematical precision to the secular calendar.[18]

The Rescue of Remnants and the Second Loss

Isolated remnants from the manuscripts survived and were passed down by inheritance to his grandson, Dr. Yosef Mohilever, who before his death delivered them to Rabbi Yehudah Leib HaKohen Maimon for publication.[18, 19] The history of the publication, reconstruction and second loss of these remnants is described in the following table:

Memorial Institutions and Long-Term Influence

The memory and work of Rabbi Shmuel Mohilever have been extensively commemorated among educational institutions, public organizations and governmental bodies in Israel.[2] The Benei Akiva yeshiva in Hadera is named
"Beit Shemuel" bears his name, and in the city of Bnei Brak the "No'am Mohaliver" school currently operates.[2] The rabbi's personal archive, which assembles unique documents, photographs, letters, and official certificates from his public and private life, is preserved and catalogued in the Central Zionist Archives in Jerusalem, and continues to serve researchers and historians of Religious Zionism.[2]

His spatial commemoration found expression not only in educational institutions, but also in the names of settlements such as the local council Mazkeret Batya, which was founded by his direct initiative and became a local council in 1952, and in Kibbutz Gan Shmuel, which maintains a historical connection to the national etrog enterprise established in his honor.[3, 7, 10]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Synthesis and Historical Assessment

The legacy of Rabbi Shmuel Mohaliver marks the historical transition of Orthodox Judaism from a posture of defensiveness and passivity to a posture of national activism and historical initiative. He did not regard the contradiction between the traditional world and modernity and nationalism as an inescapable fate, but rather as a religious challenge to be resolved through bold and dynamic halakhic tools.

Analysis of his activity demonstrates how meticulous and rationalistic Lithuanian scholarship, combined with a deeply emotional worldview, enabled him to rule halakhically with extraordinary breadth of mind. From the donation of communities for national enterprises, through the struggle over the "heter mekhirah" that saved the agriculture of the colonies, to the establishment of a political institutional infrastructure such as Mizrachi—Rabbi Mohaliver shaped the ideological framework that enabled thousands of observant Jews to integrate into the building of the Land shoulder to shoulder with secular pioneers. The research and Torah efforts continuing even today to reconstruct and publish his writings attest to the vitality of his teachings and to their unshakable centrality in understanding the growth of modern Religious Zionism.[18]
